utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. This is case number IT-95-5/18-PT, the Prosecutor versus Radovan Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you and good morning to everyone. Mr. Karadzic, you appear again on your own. Can you confirm to me, please, that you're hearing translation into your own language.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Lordship.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I have appearances, please for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. Alan Tieger, Hildegard Uertz-Retzlaff and Iain Reid for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. I issued a fairly brief agenda indicating the things that parties might at least prepare to deal with. There may be other matters that will be raised once we've gone through this. So I'll start at the beginning, and the first item relates really to -- well, it may be that it's the Prosecution that can elaborate on this for me. The Chamber was invited to reconsider its decision about how contact might be made by Mr. Karadzic and those working for him with Prosecution witnesses and agreed to reconsider in light of the fact that the parties themselves were more or less agreed on what was the appropriate course to follow. So can I be updated, please, on what has happened since that decision of the 15th of July.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, the procedures between the associates, the Prosecution, and the victim witness section have been established. There are liaison persons on all sides. The Prosecution has received a list of 85 through the witness victim section, 85 priority witnesses. For 70 of them the contact details were provided immediately. To our knowledge the victim witness unit is contacting people in relation to 15 witnesses, some details on the contacts had to be clarified. Several RFAs were filed. So it's actually progressing. In relation to the witness list for the 92 bis witnesses, I'm also aware that the Defence has sent such a list to the victim witness section and we are providing the contact details on a rolling basis. It's actually working.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, can I just firm up some of the detail. The 70, I think you mentioned that were -- sorry, 85, was it?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: 85 is the list of priority witnesses, mostly insiders actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Laying aside the ones that had to be clarified, have you a date for the transmission of the contact details to the victims and witnesses section? Can you tell me when that happened?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I think it was actually on the same day or the next day, but I'm not actually sure now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So are we talking about roughly a week ago that this has actual -- was actually happening or was it at the beginning of the week or -- of this week or what?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I would not know that. I only know that it was done immediately on the same day, actually, when we received the list actions were taken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay. And in relation to 92 bis witnesses, and you talk about the details being provided on a rolling basis, has the roll started to move?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It's starting actually today, yes, because the witness unit is actually dealing at the moment with this other 70, and -- yeah. There was -- the list had actually be changed because of the withdrawals, and this -- so a new list had to be prepared. We assisted the associate in doing this and it was then done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff. Mr. Karadzic, is there anything you wish to say on this subject?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just that we are ready the moment we receive the necessary consent and all the details to get in touch with witnesses so that either I can interview them here or my associates in Serbia or Republika Srpska or in Bosnia. And in that respect, there shall be no delay on our part. We will be ready. We have a lot of associates who are working pro bono for the time being, but we hope to settle that as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. While on the subject of witnesses, I want to look at a number of matters associated with protective measures. We are, as I think I indicated at the last Status Conference, in the course of preparing a chart that records the Trial Chamber's understanding of the protective measures which are actually in force from whatever source and apply at present in this case. We think it's helpful to resolve these issues before the trial starts. We acknowledge that because there are so many and the whole issue is so complex there may yet be inaccuracies in the chart, but if there are, I suspect they are very few and very minor. However, the parties have an opportunity very shortly to look at this chart and to make comments, and there will be an order probably issued today which will give a dead-line for responding to this. The -- yes. The likely date will be the 7th of August, so that would be two weeks from now, but it's simply a question of checking this against your own records. And while you may decide no comment is necessary because it's completely accurate, it would be helpful to be told that you had checked it and that you had found it so rather than just leave us to await the expiry of the 14 days before taking any further action, because we then propose making an order just containing the final version, which of course will have to be altered and updated as any other decisions are made not only in relation to applications that the Prosecution might make for other reasons as the trial goes on but also updated to reflect any application Mr. Karadzic may make for protective measures for any witnesses he intends to lead and also to reflect any modifications that are made, because I anticipate that he will make applications to vacate or modify the measures for certain witnesses. So it will be updated on a regular basis, but at least we will not constantly have to go back and recheck the foundation for each one if we're all agreed now on the terms of the chart. At the last meeting, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, you gave an indication that a certain number -- it was a limited number of witnesses had indicated they longer requested the protective measures which had been granted. I think there may have been only three, from memory, but there were some.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, no application has been made to vacate any of the protective measures that might have applied to such witnesses. Are you intending to make such submissions?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I thought we did, but it may have escaped my attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Nothing has been done so far, so it would be helpful if that could be done forthwith, because it's again an administrative matter that we ought to be able to resolve now. Now, Mr. Karadzic, there has been an exchange of filings about the protective measures for witnesses who have subsequently died. There were two in particular, and you eventually withdrew your request to vary these measures in light of the information given by the Prosecution, and all of that will be reflected in the order which will accompany the chart. One of the other things you asked was that the Prosecution should do the same exercise for any other witness who has since died, but you've now been advised that there are no other witnesses who fall into that category and therefore that seems to be an unnecessary request now. The request was perfectly legitimate, but now that the position has been clarified there will be no need for any action to be taken on it. Now, of before I move off the issue of -- the broad issue of witnesses and protective measures, is there anything else you wish to say on that subject? I shall come later to the question of expert witnesses, so lay them aside, but in relation to witnesses in general and protective measures, do you wish to say anything further?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Lordship, and I hope I shall never fail to file certain motions concerning protective measures, because the Defence has a position against them. It's a principled position, because we want this trial to be as transparent as possible, and we hope that it will be so and that my rights will be protected in the courtroom. And except for the victims, in relation to whose protective measures I shall not take a stand, nobody else is entitled to have protective measures, because I don't think that any harm came to anybody who was involved in these trials, especially not Serbs, and I have -- and I see no reasons, either be it for the representatives of the international organisations or for insiders to have any sort of protective measures. I hope that this trial can be a model for future trials and that things need to be done properly, and for such broad protective measures to be in existence, that really casts a shadow over these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you know from the last Status Conference that the Trial Chamber is conscious of this as an issue. How to resolve it is a matter which will be determined on a case-by-case basis as we progress. It's impossible to give effect to your general motion to vacate protective measures, but in the order I've referred to earlier, accompanying the chart, it is made clear that it's necessary to identify the witnesses that are not victims that you seek to have a change made in the protective measures for. So that's an exercise that you will have to undertake. You may need assistance from the Prosecution to identify exactly which ones are victims, but by now you've probably got enough information to do that. I know it's a time-consuming exercise, but as a result of that you'll be able to make individual applications for alteration to the protective measures which I'm sure you appreciate you have to justify. You know what the rules say about this. Where they've been granted in the past, then you would need to demonstrate a reason why they're not necessary now if the witness does not consent to them being removed. On a number of occasions at these Status Conferences you've made the sort of comment you've made already. I'm not criticising you for that, but we understand your general position about the situation being different from what it was years ago and that in your view there is no need for these measures, but any application you make will have to be more specific to the individuals involved. I'm sure you realise that. I turn now to a different subject, which is the impact of a recent decision made on judicial notice of adjudicated facts. When the first decision on judicial notice was made, the Prosecution intimated the withdrawal of certain witnesses. There's been no reaction as yet to the second decision. Can you indicate, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, what's likely to happen?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, we will file a similar motion, and we either do it today or tomorrow, and we will ask for the withdrawal of ten and -- at least ten but probably more. The discussion has not completed -- be completed yesterday, otherwise we would have done that yesterday. But at least ten, most likely more, will also be withdrawn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are any of them experts?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: To my knowledge, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: A significant body of the expert evidence relates to the identification of victims at -- of the events at Srebrenica. You don't envisage that the decisions that were made in relation to judicial notice will affect the evidence you intend to present to identify the victims or at least the number of victims?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I understand the Court's point, and all we can do at this stage -- first of all, I reiterate what Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff said. All we can do at this stage is to double-check to ensure that that specific issue was distinctly considered in the evaluation of whether or not witnesses could be placed on the reserve list, and if it -- if it turns out that, in fact, the adjudicated facts did not obviate, at least temporarily, the need to have those witnesses considered, then that's simply the case. But if it turns out that for some reason the evaluation was focussed on the witnesses themselves and not the experts, then the concerns the Court raises may -- may turn out to result in the reduction of some experts. We'll just have to check that, and I can't say at this moment whether -- I can't confirm at this moment that those experts were weighed against the adjudicated facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. Well, it follows from that, Mr. Karadzic, that the possibility of all the expert witnesses proposed actually giving evidence is a live issue, and you have had ongoing discussions with the Office of Legal Affairs and Defence here about the allocation of resources for the expert witnesses that you propose, and you're miles apart on that issue. Now, I would like to know, first of all, your view of the situation as it now is.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you see, Your Lordship, 26 expert witnesses of the OTP were not seen in any other cases, and this is yet another reason why this case is so voluminous. The witnesses -- expert witnesses of the OTP had huge resources, time and resource allocation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you there. These witnesses have mostly, if not all, given evidence in other cases.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But not all in the same case as in my case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I understand that, but they're -- yes. Well, continue with what you have to say.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Therefore, they had huge resources and opportunities to write their findings. Once again, I wish to emphasise the rule on equality of arms and resources, and I simply cannot allow for this issue to be neglected, nor can these experts allow themselves to be less than professional and provide insufficient information. What is important here, especially when it comes to the problem that you raised, the identification of victims, my experts are all professionals with reputation, university professors with long-standing experience, and they simply cannot allow themselves to make their findings on the basis of just some paperwork. They need to be supplied with additional material, forensic material and so on based on which the expert findings were written. To comment on these findings without that could only amount to whether the findings were done in a proper way or not. But to actually ascertain whether or not they're accurate, they need to do much more work. So I plead with you to make sure that this is done properly, as the Defence is assuring you that most of the surprises in this trial will come on the issue of identification of victims and so on. They think that they have made some concessions due to the volume of this case, but what is at stake here are the rules, and the rules here are wrong. The Prosecution, in this case and in this institution, can do what it wants, whereas my resources are limited, and it is impossible to strike a balance, and it is impossible for me to reply to these findings. This is the one of the most important aspects to establish the truth. I cannot go as far as to say that the Judges in this institution made erroneous mistakes, political decisions and so on, because the truth was not established. We ask that the objective truth be established, and we will show the entire situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina on very firm grounds, and it is only after that that we can discuss and conclude whether this Court is a political institution or not, but prior to that we need to ensure all of these conditions. The number of hours is a problem. There's nothing we can do in the limited number of hours at our disposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You have, of course, to bear in mind that experts that you intend to instruct have also been involved in previous cases.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not all of them, Your Lordship. Besides, I'm not sure that they had an opportunity to see all the material, because some of the material had never been disclosed. What they had were Prosecution experts' reports, and that is not enough. All they can conclude based on that is whether the reports are well written or not. They can't conclude whether they are correct or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But if you take as an example Professor Dunjic, he's given evidence on a number of occasions here, but in particular he's given evidence in relation to Srebrenica, and he sat through all the experts in the Popovic trial. Now, it can hardly be said he's coming to this task with a blank sheet. He comes with -- with a great deal of information, and he must know already where to look for the areas in which there might be a genuine dispute.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't believe that Professor Dunjic was satisfied in the previous cases with what he had been supplied with by the OTP. However, this applies even more to Professor Oliver Stojkovic who did not have any analysis of the documents referring to the material at his disposal, and he could not conclude anything. If you only look at how much resources did the 26 OTP expert witnesses have at their disposal, you can grasp the extent of this disproportion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I am surprised to hear you mention that. My understanding was that the Prosecution experts were paid less than the Defence experts for the work that they did. You seem to have a different understanding.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I am talking about is the number of hours. I believe that their number of hours was virtually limitless, and you can count those in months rather than in hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But you have to bear in mind that they were working at the grave sites, handling the remains of thousands of people, doing a quite different job from an analytical exercise in the current circumstances of the work that others had to do in dreadful circumstances. We have to bear -- you know, bring some sense of proportion to this. And I recognise that you're going to have to have a greater allocation of hours for experts in this field of pathology and forensic science than possibly in any other case that has been here, but we still have to bring a sense of proportion to bear on the issue. And it is difficult for me to get a proper understanding of what is genuinely necessary when very broad assertions are made about all that needs to be done to check work, which in the first instance was done by professionals of standing themselves and isn't just a work that has been cobbled together in an unprofessional way. Now, your experts are obviously entitled to comment on the methodology of others. They're entitled to look at examples of what they did, and perhaps by pointing to a number of examples may build a case that undermines the expert, but it doesn't on the face of it seem realistic to say that every post-mortem report ought to somehow or other be analysed in the course of this yet again by an expert for the Defence. So what I'm trying to identify or invite you to consider identifying is what's realistic rather than asserting a right which is unrealistic to examine the detail of every document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Lordship, Professor Dunjic was never provided with the reports of individual post-mortems. Professor Stojkovic never received materials from the ICMP, and now I would like to be less general and more specific. This is the last ever opportunity for us to clarify what happened in Bosnia, and particularly in Srebrenica. I assure you that we are talking about the differences that can be numbered in the thousands of victims, thousands, not tens. Creating a myth on erroneous facts about Srebrenica can cost Europe as well, because this gives legitimacy to a number of erroneous facts that they can turn the anger of the general public against Europe, and this cannot be clarified if we believe that one expert was wrong about one case. We want to be absolutely sure who was victim there and how many there were. If we miss that opportunity now, Europe will also feel that as a major problem. This is not a matter of principle. That is matter of us trying to establish the fact, and if we do that, I don't even care what the Trial Chamber's decision will be about me. I just want to find the truth and we can't do that based on examples and a sample. And this is the least sacrifice that this court can do to allow my experts to see every single piece of material, all the DNA analysis, individual post-mortems, and then we will end up with the true list, the correct list of victims which will differ by thousands in respect of what is believed at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let's look at from the other side. We're talking about events 14 years ago. Presumably you've been gathering material provided by experts who have looked at this from the opposite point of view, to try to establish that what is presented to the public is a myth. Now, have you not already got that material together, your experts identified who can present the argument that the genocide, the alleged genocide did not occur and that it is all misrepresentation?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Until I arrived here, I did not collect anything, because I had struck a deal with the international community that I would not be indicted and brought to trial. And on the other hand, my experts cannot rely on newspaper information. They need to have the same material that the OTP experts were privy to in order to be able to see whether the facts were established correctly and whether the conclusions were established correctly. That's why my experts have to focus on the same body of material that their counterparts had. This is the only way. They must be able to see everything that the OTP experts saw and then they will be able to confront them with their expert views. Anything else would be incorrect vis-a-vis history, reconciliation, the peoples involved, victims, and the international justice. All sorts of things are happening there. The graves are being dug out. Bodies are being moved to Srebrenica in order to prove a point. This is our last opportunity to establish the truth, and in that, Srebrenica is a very significant point in case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let me clarify with the Prosecution just the state of play so far as provision of material is concerned. Who is dealing with this issue? Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, Dr. Karadzic is indicating that there maybe material sought which has not been provided. Can you help me on what exchanges have taken place about this?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, there were quite some exchanges about the materials that are actually not in custody of the Prosecution which are actually with the experts or, rather, with the organisation they work with, and we have actually proposed to have a meeting with the associates to clarify a few things in relation to that. The Prosecution cannot -- as this institution, this external organisation, is independent, we cannot order them to do certain things. We can only facilitate contacts. It's about the provision of 300 -- as far as I understand it, 300 probes. It's about 300 probes that the Defence experts want to do, and there seems to be -- this seems to be quite --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What do you mean --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Probing DNA. They actually want to go to the real DNA evidence and want to make probes to establish whether the methodology of the Prosecution experts is correct, and there seems to be a real -- first a matter of confidentiality of this information, which is the position of that external institution, and the other issue is that it would be very time-consuming, but that's something that we, as the Prosecution, have no real input in. It's the between the Defence and these external experts. But we try to facilitate it, and we have proposed a meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But there must be some substance in the suggestion that the Defence should be able to run some tests similar to those done by the organisation you refer to with a view to checking the accuracy of what was actually done by them.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. We actually have the same view, but it's a question of how many and -- but that's not for us to judge. It's a rather a matter of the expert. How many probes would you make to -- to -- would you have to do to establish that methodology is correct? So whether it should be 300, I don't know. We can't say that. It sounds to me quite a lot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, but you also sounded earlier as though you were lying down to the idea that there's an issue of confidentiality here and that you weren't perhaps asserting as a Prosecutor that in fairness there is a point at which confidentiality has to be interfered with. I mean, we're not talking about confidentiality in the sense of, I think, affecting people -- people's current daily lives. We're talking about a different type of confidentiality.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's not a matter that -- that Prosecution raises. It's actually a matter that the organisation raises --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand that, but --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: -- and we cannot actually -- we have -- we cannot order them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Why can't you influence them, persuade them? I -- it sounded to me as though you were accepting that that's their position and we just have to accept it; whereas you're the person in control of the -- the presentation of a case, and you know that if the Defence do not have a fair chance of challenging that case that the evidence might be excluded, and you've got quite a strong hand in explaining to one of your providers or -- evidence providers or indeed a witness that certain things have to be conceded in the interests of a fair trial.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, we actually did that. We had conversations, and we actually did that, and it's not that this organisation doesn't want to do it but they want -- they need to go back to the victims' families from where the DNA was taken, because it was taken under the premise that it would not be provided elsewhere. So they have to go back. That's at least their understanding of their duties. They have to go back to these providers of the DNA and confirm with them that it can be provided to Dr. Karadzic, and that's -- that's the issue, and if it is 300 probes, then it is quite a lot of work for them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I find it difficult to understand that a person might consent to have material given to a Prosecutor and not realise that the inevitable result of that must be that the Defence would have a pretty strong claim at least for access to it. It seems a strange situation if they've already consented to you having it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: But I can only comment to you what the discussion was and that they need -- need to go back to the people providing the DNA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I hope you've checked the terms of the consent that was originally given and are satisfied that this is absolutely necessary, because it's clearly yet another thing that may well cause a delay here. So this requires urgent attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, is that the only area of discussion about the provision of additional material?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That's -- the DNA is the centre of the entire discussion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just remind me of the main point behind the use of DNA evidence in this case where we don't, I think, have a schedule, for example, of identified victims and we're working largely on numbers rather than individual identities.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: That's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does it have a big impact on the case?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: To our knowledge actually not, Your Honour, because -- that's why we also were very surprised why it was focusing on the DNA, because even if there were mistakes among those identifications, to -- to us it was actually no doubt that the people in the mass graves were actually the men and boys from Srebrenica. Therefore, we were actually rather surprised that the DNA suddenly became such an important point for Mr. Karadzic. That's why we actually thought the witnesses -- these expert witnesses were 92 bis witnesses; they wouldn't even have to come, because -- I don't know. I see now to see that the position of Mr. Karadzic is that the people in the mass graves are actually not the boys and men from Srebrenica. I seem to understand that this is what the Defence line would be, but that's -- that's new to me. I didn't actually inspect that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When do you anticipate the meeting that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We have proposed it already last week, and there was something holding it up. We have, therefore, not have made a concrete appointment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you saying the difficulty lies with the provider or with the associates of Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We -- yeah. I would say the latter. I mean, we have conversations -- rather, e-mail communication with the associates about this meeting, but it never materialised to a particular date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It would actually already be helpful if the associate would meet with us. There is not necessarily to have to be the organisation there as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, what do you have to say in response to that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With all due respect for Mrs. Retzlaff, I can't agree that the Defence is a third party. The Defence is the second inevitable party to these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The third party she's referring to is the ICMP and not the Defence. She's saying that the -- they may need not to be present when they first have a meeting, that that meeting should be with one of your associates.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. I believe that this referred to the fact that they were DNA material providers, and they were not prepared to disclose that to a third party, and the third party in this case was Defence. I can't understand another thing. The OTP gave those institutions the task to carry out a job, and the owner of the material is the OTP, not the institutions. I can't accept when I hear that the OTP cannot have the material given back to them, and I really can't understand how come the OTP offers only 300 samples to us. We want the entire material, and we will take a random sample and choose 300, and if there are major discrepancies among the 300, then we will broaden the sample and continue the procedure. Furthermore, I have an objection to the terms as used for boys and men. I believe that this has to be clarified in writing. We have to define what the term "boys" implies. We do not believe that a conclusion can be made on a number. I believe that in criminal matters a body has to be present. Here in several cases against the Albanians it was concluded that without a body murder charges cannot be proven. We have to establish the truth. When somebody died, whether they died in 1992, 1993, or 1995; whether they were killed in combat or whether they were killed as a result of executions. I believe that for thousands of them we can assume that people's hands were tied, and based on that we can assume that those people were executed, but this is a generalisation which cannot be used to establish the guilt of an entire people, not only one person. I'm talking about this approach. It is hard to believe that they cannot disclose materials to us, that they cannot obtain the materials from the company from which they commissioned work. We are trying not to intervene through the Chamber, but in any case, we can certainly not give up on our desire to establish the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: First thing, though, seems to be a meeting which attempts have been made to arrange and for some reason has not taken place. Now, can you help me on that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were some meetings. I know that there were some meetings. In the last month we received over 105.000 pages. We're grateful for that and we're working on that, but that is not the entire material that we need. Very significant portions are missing. Unfortunately, if there are claims about primary, secondary, and tertiary graves, then one DNA can come up in a number of cases. So the figures mean nothing. We need to know the clear identity. My associates will be available for the meeting, but the purpose of the meeting should not be to avoid disclosing the material, and in that sense, I cannot authorise my associates to accept such a meeting the purpose of which is to ensure that we will not receive the material. The condition for the meeting must be disclosure, full disclosure, and we shall abide by all the rules concerning the protection of data and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's a bit simpler than that, Mr. Karadzic. If they don't cooperate in a reasonable way on your instructions with a view to securing their objective, then the Court will have no sympathy for the position you take. A meeting is being suggested. There are no preconditions, as I understand it, although there may be a point of view to be presented by the Prosecution and by the ICMP, but there's little going to be achieved by taking firm positions before a meeting and then allowing them to interfere with the meeting taking place at all. Now, I'd like to understand, if you are willing to assist me, where this line takes you in your defence. Is it purely a question of numbers, that the argument based on DNA will be that the numbers have been grossly exaggerated? Or is it some other number that were -- contained in the reports, allegations that -- or findings that people were victims from Srebrenica that are inaccurate?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Everything in relation to Srebrenica that has been presented so far is erroneous. There are people coming up now, living people whose names are on the tombstones. In the first elections, there were people who voted who had been listed as missing and killed. There were people who fell victims in combat throughout the entire period, and people who died in 1992 on 1993 were later on portrayed as victims of massacre in Srebrenica. So everything is contentious and everything needs to be established fact by fact. There were huge combats in forests after the fall or liberation of Srebrenica. These victims cannot be treated as victims of the massacre. The civilian authorities in Srebrenica accepted the surrender, and the military elements continued fierce fighting in order to break through the Serbian lines and Serbian territories. So we do not have a clear picture, and we may not allow for this to remain this way, because so far we have not established the truth. In addition to that, there are many people living abroad who were listed as missing. So all of that needs to be established. As for the sample that my experts will make from the entire DNA material, the sample of 300 random sample materials, that will clearly show what the situation is. This is of huge importance both for Serbian and for the Muslim nation and for Europe and for the international law. My associates are here -- or, rather they're here three days a month. Only one of my associates is permanently in The Hague and the rest of them live in other areas, and they're authorised to come here only three days a month.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But please try to assist me on the point I'm trying to clarify. How does dip sampling the DNA tests help you to establish that people died in fighting or combat or that their -- people are living abroad who have been listed -- how does dip sampling DNA deal with any of that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You see, Your Lordship, we are convinced that there is a multifold exaggeration here. We wish to establish exactly who perished and whose DNA was provided in order to be able to say that, yes, this number of victims is beyond contention. My experts know what they're doing. They saw summary reports that mean nothing. All they can conclude is whether their grammar was correct when writing those findings, but the truth cannot be established that way. Our associates replied to the Prosecution, and they said that they needed that material so that our expert Stojkovic could do his work. Following that, the meetings would be more useful. Such a number of victims is bandied about, and the material provided is of a summary nature, and we believe that we cannot establish the truth unless we're provided the entire material. I have mentioned primary, secondary, and tertiary graves. One DNA could have been portrayed three times representing three persons and we need to verify everything. We need to let that run through the computer, through software, in order to establish what this is all about, and you will see what the truth about Srebrenica will look like following this trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I must say I don't really understand very much of this. You've just made an allegation that one DNA could have been portrayed three times representing three people. What do you mean by that? Are you saying that people are falsifying DNA results, the professionals that did it in the first place? Or is this just a hopeful assertion that you're making? I mean, what basis have you for this sort indication, and what exactly does it mean?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Lordship, this is just a possibility. It's a possibility that nobody can exclude at this point. I'm not going as far as to say that somebody is doing this on purpose, knowingly. We wish to examine this methodology and we wish to follow the same method, the same path that was used by the experts of the Prosecution, and only then we'll be able to say this is why it's wrong or this is why it's accurate. At this point this is a possibility and nobody can exclude it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What can be said is that there's a willingness on the part of the Prosecution to facilitate your request, and that can only be fulfilled if your associate is instructed forthwith to arrange first of all to meet with the Prosecution and, if necessary, to meet with them and the ICMP. So I expect urgent attention to be given to that suggestion.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Tieger just alerted me to the last e-mail that we actually got from Mr. Sladojevic where he addresses the reason why he couldn't have the meeting, and what he actually says in this e-mail from the 21st of July, he says, "We will get back to you as soon as OLAD has made a decision in relation to expert hours to be authorised." This is his reason, claim, in the e-mail why he hasn't met yet. So just to say that. And one other point I would like to also clarify. The ICMP did also not provide the DNA to us. They have it. So it's not that they give it to us and not to others. That was a misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I understand the point that Sladojevic may have been making in that e-mail, but it's a misconception that the meeting which has been proposed should not take place pending the determination of the allocation of hours. They are two separate issues. I appreciate the work might not be capable of being done in the way that you particularly want it done unless the appropriate allocation is made, but that's no reason for holding up the negotiations to get the material. So please instruct him that that meeting should take place forthwith. Meanwhile, you know that I am going to take certain steps in relation to the allocation of hours, and these will be to express for OLAD my understanding of the situation that's emerged from this discussion this morning, and in light of that, I am certain that there will be some change to the allocation, but it's for them to decide what the allocation is in the light of all the information that's provided to them. In principle, it seems to me that an exercise that dip samples the DNA work done on behalf of the Prosecution or of which the Prosecution are going to make use is a reasonable investigation for the Defence to carry out, and the assessment must mainly concentrate on the extent of that exercise.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may, Your Lordship. I wish to clarify something concerning the meetings. Namely, this is not an issue of principle; this is a practical issue. Mr. Sladojevic has no business in that meeting until he receives a report from Stojkovic as to what is missing. And in order for Stojkovic to send a report on what is missing he must receive the hours allocated to him for that purpose. So it's a matter of substance, not a matter of us doing this to spite somebody. It is in everybody's interest to do it as soon as possible, but as soon as we have everything that we need for Stojkovic to say, "This is what I'm missing," then Mr. Sladojevic can say in the meeting, "This is what we're missing." There is no purpose in meeting unless some result is going to be achieved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Has Stojkovic not already had an allocation of hours made to him?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that it has been just resolved, but he needs time to review that and to inform Sladojevic about what is missing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You see, your position now is different from what I understood it a little time ago. Earlier you said -- or at least Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff said, and you confirmed, that you were seeking 300 examples. You would prefer to have the whole of the material, and you would make the selection of the 300. But on either view, it was a question of 300 samples. Now, are you telling me that that's not what you want, that it's not yet clear what you want? Because that's what you seem now to be saying.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. Mr. Stojkovic has his first task to review everything that has been disclosed and to say, "This is what is missing." And it is then that Mr. Sladojevic will be able to say, "This is what we're still lacking, will you please disclose that to us." Once Mr. Stojkovic receives the entire material, then we will ask for the entire DNA material to be supplied, not reports but the DNA material, the results. And out of all the available DNA, my team -- or, rather, Mr. Stojkovic and Mr. Dunjic, will make a random sample of 300, which is less than 10 per cent of the -- well, I don't know. Two and a half thousand have been identified, and we hear numbers such as 8.000, 10.000 bandied about. Next year I'm sure it will be 15.000. So they will make a 10 per cent random sample, and my team needs to select this sample, not the team of the Prosecution. And if in that sample there is no distortion, no deviation, then they will make one conclusion; and if there is significant statistical deviation, then they will ask for the entire material to be supplied in order to establish the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's how I understood your position to be and it doesn't seem to me that Mr. Stojkovic needs to do anything for you to have a meeting with the Prosecution, so I reiterate what I said earlier, that I expect that meeting to make place forthwith.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I suppose that we will need one week longer than the dead-line in August in order to provide the reply, because not everything has been disclosed to us. The disclosure is not complete. It's quite chaotic. And I do not want to blame the Prosecution for that, but most likely those who work for them are faulty. It is very difficult to classify that material. The material is quite chaotic. Hundred and five thousand pages. We would need I don't know how many days to go over that material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does that mean you intend to submit another response to the motion for admission of the expert witness evidence under Rule 92 bis?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, after we review everything, but our dead-line is sometime in August, I think, and I think we will be one week short in order to provide a complete answer. Our dead-line is in August to reply concerning that issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm regarding that, Mr. Tieger, as an application to extend the dead-line for the response to the Prosecution motion for admission of the evidence of eight experts by seven days, to the 20th of August. It presently is the 13th of August. Do you have anything to say on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In principle, Your Honour, I wouldn't ordinarily object to a continuance. I would like to take a moment, however, to consider the basis for that. I'm not aware that -- at least offhand, that complaints about the provision of materials were previously made and formed a basis for an application for continuance, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But you do have the odd expert who is responsible for literally thousands of pages of report. Haglund, for example, comes in a five-volume series covering different sites, so there may be substance in the suggestion that time is necessary to review this material.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I'm not rejecting it reflectively. My concerns arise from simply the fact that we have been advised on a couple of occasions, more than a couple of occasions, that materials weren't provided and it turns out that they were. But in any event, I take the Court's point. There's no -- there's no -- we don't object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't think that's really the point. It was the chaotic provision this time, but that's --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In any event, there's no objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I will extend the time for response in the case of the motion for admission of the evidence of eight experts from the 13th to the 20th of August as you request.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Lordship.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Apart from that motion, are there another 92 bis motions to which you will make further responses, bearing in mind that you submitted an omnibus response which indicated you were unlikely to say any more?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Lordship, the omnibus motion, I hope, can be used as grounds to postpone the decision on admissibility until we are complete -- until we have completed our work. Otherwise, we would just be burdening and introducing too much material into the case. This is why we resorted to this omnibus response. For us to say that something is acceptable we need to be sure whether there is something that has remained unresolved, and our investigation and our discussion with the witnesses will clarify that completely. If the Prosecution objects to that, they can shorten the proceedings and take these people from the 92 bis list and call them to testify here live. If there is no time, then that's the avenue we should take rather than wait for us to see whether we can accept something without cross-examination; or we can respond individually for each particular case, but in that case we will have 213 or 217 such responses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's been drawn to my attention, Mr. Tieger and Mr. Karadzic, that the date I was working on for the response to the motion about eight experts was the date in the original order giving dead-lines, that there is a revised dead-line of the 25th of August already. So an additional week takes you to the 1st of September and not to the 20th of August. So that extension gives you until the 1st of September. As presently advised, the Trial Chamber is unlikely to make decisions about the admission of evidence under Rule 92 bis during the pre-trial phase. I anticipate that the 92 bis motions will be dealt with when the Trial Chamber to conduct the case is assigned. The other motions, however, that fall under 92 quater may be dealt with differently. Now, it follows from that, Mr. Karadzic, that if there were circumstances in which you had additional material to respond in relation to any of the 92 bis motions that you would be able to do so until a decision had been made. At least you would be able to ask the Chamber to accept further information up until the time the motion was determined.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Lordship.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Prosecution filed on the 17th of July a request for reconsideration of the refusal by the Chamber to allow them to reply to your response in the 92 quater motion about KDZ-198. Do you have anything to say on the subject of whether the Trial Chamber should reconsider that decision and allow the Prosecution to reply to the points you made, which were a number of points about the reliability of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Lordship, if the Prosecution believes this to be necessary, to have yet another paper, then we will not object to that. We simply would not be opposed to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We should probably have assumed that that would be your position. It's consistent with what position you've taken in other similar situations. A decision will be issued allowing a reply. It will be filed today. So -- and I assume the reply is ready and can come in tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. It can actually come in today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we'll give you until tomorrow just in case. Mr. Karadzic, the Prosecution have also submitted a motion asking for an order that you return certain ex parte material. I think I need to go into private session to deal with that in case we get into the detail of it, in which case we would need to be doing it in private. So I'm going into private session now. If it turns out that that's unnecessary, we'll come straight back into open session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, tell me what you mean by the batch number that you need.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] An ERN number doesn't mean much because I don't have a search engine. I don't have that software. However, on CDs they are marked until batch 96. The last I received was 96 with -- containing some ICMP material. So if I were provided with a CD number rather than an ERN number, it would be easier for me to find it. Searching a hundred CDs is much easier than searching close to a million pages, as you will appreciate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, can you oblige on the first one?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, it's the batch number 61, and you got this on the 21st of April this year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And then in relation to the second and third items?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's actually specified in the motion. It's an item -- a filing that was provided by the registry in error. So two ex parte items were provided in error.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the first one in paragraph 5 refers again to a CD, but that won't be a CD with a number like the number you've just given us.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, because that's actually a distribution from the registrar related -- but it should also be easily to find because it's related to a particular motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you'll see there, Mr. Karadzic -- well, you may not have this document with you, but we're talking about appendices which were ex parte appendices accompanying the Prosecution's seventh 92 bis motion, and that relates to delayed disclosure of witness identity, and that was -- now, do you keep -- do you keep motions in a particular place so that you can go to it and find this one?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a lot of papers. I gave some to my associates. I will look for them. My associates will never disclose anything confidential or ex parte. The matter with the electronic batch 61, you consider it done. If I knew that number, I would have returned the material on the first day. I will go and look through my papers, but you can't even imagine how much paper I have. Although I receive electronic material I still have a lot of papers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Your associates have returned the material that they got. It's only your copy that's in issue here. So please look for that. That was the seventh 92 bis motion. Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, do you have a date when that was filed? Oh, 29th of May, I think. Yes. 29th of May it was filed. Now, I really don't want to get into exchanging paperwork on a subject like this. I note your assurance about the CD. I note what you've said about the other two items. I'm going to order just now that in the event that they are not all returned to the Prosecution by Monday, that they should notify the Chamber, and the Chamber will deal with the motion; but hopefully, the Prosecution will by Monday able to intimate that these have been returned and that the motion can be withdrawn. We've reached the stage, I think, where we do need to have a break for the purposes of the management of the court. The only thing remaining on this agenda is a discussion about Rule 90 -- sorry, Rule 73 bis. Now, an order was issued yesterday with an annex or a schedule attached to it. I just want to look at certain examples from that and have a brief discussion about how they might be dealt with to give some guidance on what's expected by the Chamber in response to this. So we will adjourn now and resume at 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I turn now to an order that was issued yesterday which is designed to focus attention on the Pre-Trial Conference and any other discussions leading up to the Pre-Trial Conference, and it reflects concern that the volume of this case may be such that steps may be required to limit the Prosecution case. Now, there are a number of methods or means available to the Trial Chamber to control the overall length of the case, but of course it may turn out that that's not necessary depending on the way in which it is ultimately presented; but the Trial Chamber needs to know before the trial starts what's likely to emerge and how long and complex it is likely to be. There's already some basic information available which is reflected in the order. We know that the Prosecution are talking about a case which would involve examination-in-chief of Prosecution witnesses of approximately 490 hours. We know that they have in mind, I think, something like 560 witnesses, and we know that the case consists of a number of episodes, and within at least one of these, there are clearly distinct areas involving individual municipalities and events within these municipalities. So this order focuses attention on the various things that could be done to ensure that the trial is not unduly lengthy and unduly complex. Now, the Trial Chamber has to rely to a significant extent on the information that the parties can give to enable it to make an appropriate decision, and there's no point in parties simply coming along with entrenched views and not looking at options, because Rule 73 bis provides a number of options, and what the Trial Chamber wishes the parties, but most particularly the Prosecution in this instance, to do is focus attention on all of these to the extent that they can see ways in which they might be of assistance in ensuring that the trial is not only fair but also expeditious. Now, one of the things that may be done to reduce the scope of the trial is either for the number of counts featuring in the trial to be reduced or the number of crime sites featuring in the trial to be reduced, and the order has attached to it various columns in a schedule identifying the crimes that are charged in the indictment. Now, when I say that this extends to 88 pages, it can readily be understood what potential there is for the trial extending unduly in time or emerging as unduly complex, and within that schedule alone some indication is given of areas where there may be helpful clarification provided by the Prosecution. I want to look at a couple of these. I'll just mention them at the moment, because obviously the parties have to take time to digest this and then to compose any response that they wish to make. In the indictment there are a number of schedules, and one of these is Schedule C, and Schedule C is simply a list of places which are described as detention facilities. Now, within the indictment there are allegations of killings, at least of conduct, rather, in these detention facilities, and if I can focus on one paragraph of the indictment. Take as an example -- if you have the indictment there, Mr. Tieger, it's paragraph 60 and subparagraph (b), which refers to: "Torture, beatings, and physical and psychological abuse during and after takeovers in the Municipalities and in detention facilities in the Municipalities, including those detention facilities listed in Schedule C, as cruel or inhumane treatment." Now, we already have a situation in relation to that paragraph where the schedule is confined to identifying the detention facilities. There's no reference to the personnel who may have been the subject of the torture, beatings, and physical and psychological abuse, and on top of that we then have the expression "including those detention facilities listed in Schedule C." Now, I can understand that the actual identification of individuals may be achieved through the witness statements. I don't think it's mentioned in the pre-trial brief, but no doubt the accused has been given the statements of the witnesses who will speak to this and therefore the case is disclosed in that way, but you have and it's a frequent feature of the indictment, the words "including those detention facilities." So, in the chart or the schedule attached to the order, the assumption has been made by the Trial Chamber that that particular paragraph is confined to those detention facilities that are mentioned, and that at least as a starting point we might not expect evidence relating to other detention facilities which are not mentioned. Is that a fair assumption, or is that one you need to think about and respond to in your written response?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, first of all, I'm not going to reject the opportunity to provide a more reflective response as the Court just suggested, but I would simply note that I think paragraph 60(b) -- I agree that the detention facilities -- well, I think by the very terms of 60(b) it does indicate that facilities beyond Schedule C were implicated or there would be no particular reason to frame it in that way. Nevertheless, as invited by the Court, I think digesting both the concerns the Court has just expressed, and I gather will continue to identify, is probably more prudent than offering an immediate reaction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You will appreciate there are 27 municipalities mentioned, I think, in that schedule, and some of them that are multi-detention facilities. Maybe they're not all mentioned. Let me check. Yes, I think they are all mentioned in that particular schedule, and there are multi-facilities in many of them. Now, there's surely enough in there as a starting point for your case, and you'll appreciate my concern if "including" is going to be relied on as indicating more. And the reason I raise is it is not because it just appears there but it appears, for example, in relation to Schedule D which is to do with cultural property and -- or cultural monuments and sacred sites, and you have general averments in the indictment about looting of private and public property and damage to private and public property, and when you refer to the public property, you again have a reference to cultural monuments and sacred sites, including, and then we have the ones which appear in Schedule D. Now, it's again a very extensive list, and the assumption has been made, and no doubt as you've indicated you'll respond in due course, but the assumption is made that the case is to be confined to the ones which have actually been identified.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes. And I think the Court is also aware -- again, thank you again for that, Your Honour. We will respond in due course. I'll simply mention at this point the fact that -- I mean one of the points I -- well, let me just say simply with respect to that the widespread and systematic nature of what occurred during this period of time is a factor for a number of reasons, not simply because of the term of art but because it's a reflection of a pattern that reveals a great deal about knowledge, command and control, notice, and so on, and so it appears in the indictment and appears not only in this case but has appeared in previous cases for a variety of reasons not necessarily related to holding the accused specifically to account for each and every crime he may be criminally responsible but for other evidential reasons as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But it's also, I think, widespread or systematic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And of course, that distinction may also be important to you, because if you focus too much on the widespread then that's when you end up, I think, with something that could be out of control. You know, as we get nearer to the trial in this case it becomes clearer and clearer just how voluminous the material that's ultimately been accumulated is, and no doubt that this trial, if it had taken place 12 or 13 years ago would not have included so much material, but we now have to accept that we've got to a point where so much more is known and is available and has to be addressed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I agree. And I also agree that there's a balance to be struck. I would -- it seem -- since the Court raises the point, let me say -- and I'm sure the Court appreciates this too and didn't mean to suggest otherwise, the aggregation of materials over the course of that period of time I think can only be considered as a good thing and a way of better informing the Court of what happened so that a better decision can ultimately be made. And as the Court expressed at the last Status Conference, it's up to the parties to identify creative ways to ensure that the maximum amount of information is made available to the Court. Now, one of the ways, I think, the Court is focusing on at the moment is let's separate the wheat from the chaff and let's focus on the most important aspects and I understand that and we'll not enter into this exercise without any prejudges. However, another way, and the Prosecution, I think, has been vigorous about attempting to ensure the maximum application of this mechanism, is through such means as 92 bis. I mean, that is, in fact, one of the mechanisms devised by this institution to ensure just that, that the maximum amount of information gets to the Court so that the best possible decision can be made, and it's made in a way that focuses precisely on nature of these cases, that is, cases involving mass crimes, and the recognition that the principle of oral testimony may in fact inhibit the receipt of the best information under those circumstances. And it focuses on elimination of the acts and conduct of the accused from 92 bis so that that can be focussed on during the course of the oral presentation of evidence. And it is for that reason, I think one of the extremely efficient mechanisms devised by this institution to fulfil precisely the objective identified by the Court in the last Status Conference, and we hope that that will be utilised to the fullest extent in the course of this case, and we have done our best to ensure that possibility. So we -- that's a recognition of our commitment to that process as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But it heralds for me -- it suggests to me that you might be less keen on looking at how Rule 73 bis might be used, and I'm coming to that view because you're pointing to things that are already being done to -- with a view to cutting the trial down to size, but you should not rely exclusively on what has been done already or proposed already or what you think might be done in relation to these motions. You must assist the Trial Chamber to reach the right conclusion by being positive in your own approach to these possible means of -- of controlling the trial that are in 73 bis. Because you assist the Chamber by pointing out how a particular method in there might be used, it doesn't follow that it will be applied against what you see as your particular interest. There's nothing to stop you telling the Chamber that you have no -- in fact, you're very much against the use of a particular device, but if it is in the mind of the Chamber, then here is how it might best be used to identify crime sites, for example, that are reasonably representative of the indictment, and it's that kind of assistance that the Chamber encourages you to give so that the full panoply is available to it with all the supporting information necessary to make the right decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No. I understand, Your Honour, and we would certainly recognise that 73 bis is another provision in the rules. We -- I wasn't merely mentioning it as lip-service when I said we won't enter into this exercise with any pre-judgements. We understand our obligation to assist the Court in every way and we will attempt to do so in this particular exercise as well. As the Court notes, we won't hesitate to alert the Court if we think the -- a more limited application of that provision is more appropriate. Similarly, we won't hesitate to alert the Court if we find that there are areas where 73 bis does advance the objective of a fair and expeditious trial in precisely the way the Court hopes. So I'm not coming to any prejudgement on this at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And remember in your deliberations on this that the big problem for a Trial Chamber in applying 92 bis is dispensing with cross-examination. The rules now allow, obviously, under a different rule, 92 ter, the presentation of the bulk, if not all, of the evidence in chief of a witness in writing, and cross-examination is often seen as an essential part of a fair trial in relation to particular evidence, and that will have a bearing on the decisions that are made under 92 bis. It doesn't mean that the result will be the presentation viva voce in live court time of all the evidence of a witness. It may have to be done a different way, more constructively, the use of reports, the restriction of cross-examination. All of these are available to the Trial Chamber as well, but there will undoubtedly be some of your 92 bis applications to which that approach is taken, and that's not to prejudge any of them. So you cannot, I think, rely on a complete success on that front.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I understand. I think a maximal success would satisfy the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, just a couple of other examples to show you our concern. If you look at paragraph 68 where we're dealing with deportation and inhumane acts, there the charge relates to both forcible transfer and deportation. And then if you go to 74, we have reference to both forcible transfer and deportation, and that's in relation to Srebrenica, which is part of what's covered in paragraph 68. It's Srebrenica and the municipalities. And then if you look at 75, there the reference is to acts of forcible transfer with no reference to deportation. Now, that may well be intended, but that's the sort of detail that we invite you to pay attention to in assisting us to identify, in case it's necessary, what is reasonably representative of the indictment. And then if I can mention just another -- I think another two examples. In Schedule C, if you look at item number 26, and the reference there to Planjo's house, and it was a detention facility at least from August until December 1992. And if you go back to Schedule B and look at number 19 of Schedule B, you'll see dates which extend beyond the period that it's said to be a detention facility in Schedule C. Now, we've highlighted a number of areas of concern in the schedule just to -- I'm not suggesting that's a complete list, but where we've identified particular potential inconsistencies in the scheduling and in the pleading and the indictment so that you would comment on these in particular. And then just the final example. If you look at paragraph 60(f). 60(f) relates to forcible transfer or deportation from homes with the municipalities and from Srebrenica. And then if you look at (i) and (j), neither of these makes any reference to Srebrenica, and that may be deliberate. And (j) also does not refer to private property in relation to any of the municipalities, and that may be deliberate. But there -- you know, when you start looking very closely at compiling a complete list of the crimes charged, you come across these uncertainties as a Trial Chamber, because the Trial Chamber doesn't have the entire picture at the moment that you have of the -- of the case. So these are reasons for inviting you to provide the assistance that's called for in this order.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I ask for a quick point of clarification?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Perhaps I didn't read the order either as carefully as I might have or certainly not in light of the Court's comments just now, but it occurs to me that -- at least at the time I read it initially, the kinds of clarification that the Court has just sought with respect to paragraph 60 would not necessarily have arisen from the focus indicated in the order, that is -- and I'm not -- my concern is not that the Court didn't spell it out carefully enough for me in that particular context. As I say, the problem may have been the way I read it, but I just want to make sure that we are focusing on what the Court wants us to focus on and don't respond with an insufficient submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The way these tie together in that particular example, Mr. Tieger, is that if you were looking for a number of crime sites that included damage to private property, then it would appear that in relation to both -- to all of the municipalities there doesn't appear to be in that paragraph a reference to private property, and that may be deliberate, but it's -- to avoid any misunderstanding, it's important to look at exactly what is said and not to assume too much because of the use of the word "including," although that doesn't arise here but it's an example of how you can read more into a charge than the Chamber is doing at the moment. I've certainly found in the past that it's been perfectly adequate to ignore the impact of the word "including" because of the number and extent of the specified examples that have been referred to in indictments in this Tribunal. So while this is, as you rightly point out, focussed on identifying ways in which the scope of the trial may be reduced, one of these is reducing the number of crime sites, or, obviously, reducing the number of counts, and part of the exercise, if that is to be done, is ensuring that everyone is clear what the end result is, what's in and what's out if that's what happens. So we took the opportunity of trying to identify areas which could usefully be clarified at this stage. Now, is there anything else you want to say on this order before I ask Mr. Karadzic for comments?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: There is, Your Honour. Thank you. The Court -- well, I've just committed myself, quite appropriately, to ensuring that the Prosecution does the best job it can in response to the Court's order. The Court mentioned earlier, "You'll obviously need time to digest the material and compose a response." I think the three weeks allotted under ordinary circumstances would be appropriate, but I have to tell the Court we cannot -- the timing is such that we can't fulfil our obligation here at this point, and the reason is simply the court recess, because of the work plan, the dead-lines, the anticipated commencement of trial after the court recess, this is a time when various leaves were allotted to the team in this compressed period of time, and the team is essentially disbanded. Even Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff and I will be gone for limited periods of time, but we -- there will be very little overlap, and certainly very little overlap with the core members of the team during that period of time. That's not to say that no work can be done, but at a minimum, I would ask that the Court extend the dead-line at least two weeks beyond the point at which the team re-assembles after the recess and that would mean August 31st.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. Tieger. Anything else?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I have one more matter to raise, not directly in connection with this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'll come back to that. Dr. Karadzic, the order is mainly aimed at the Prosecution, but the tradition in the Tribunal is to hear the Defence on issues like this and not to confine it to the Prosecution. Is there anything at this stage you want to say on the various things I've been discussing with Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for keeping the rule audiatur et altera pars, and I'm going to take any such opportunity given to me. From my point of view, any reductions in the indictment that you have in mind, the best reduction would be to withdraw the indictment completely, but I don't think that the OTP is going to do that. Since I'm not defending myself from liberty, I would be inclined to have the simplification of the indictment from the point of view of general interest, the interest of the people who have already been convicted based on some incidents and erroneously established facts. I would like to have every incidence that happened during the civil war in Bosnia-Herzegovina re-examined. If anything is reduced, I have already spent significant time on any such things that may be excluded from the indictment. There is nothing for me to say with respect to that. As for what my learned friend said about the information that the Trial Chamber needs, the Trial Chamber needs as much information as possible, not unilaterally produced. That's why I'm very cautious with regard to Rule 92 bis. The Trial Chamber needs as much information on both sides, but correct information. I don't know how viva voce testimony can muddle things up. It can only clarify things even further. What I need -- want to do, is I want to call 92 bis witnesses and make up for their interviews, and I may even be agreeable to not calling some of them. I have seen your order, Your Honour, and I have noticed something that gave me great joy. You yourself have noticed that there are positions there to the effect there's several red ones killed, several blue ones and it is not specified who killed whom and how many people were killed. I'm not going to accept that without specifying and clarifying who, when, how. You can't have an utterance somebody killed somebody else. I am in favour of re-examining every incident. I know that some people have been sentenced to a life -- to life in prison because of a -- the Markale incident, and I intend to prove that they are not guilty. I am not against a broad indictment as long as the Defence is permitted to produce any piece of evidence they want.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
