utterances.text: Well, the Defence will be allowed to produce and lead relevant evidence and the criminal responsibility of others may not be relevant in the circumstances of your trial. What is relevant is whether the incident took place and perhaps how it took place, but the extent to which you may examine the evidence that was led against individuals is another matter. The incidental effect, of course, of proving that -- or demonstrating that an incident happened in a way different from that found before would reflect on individuals who have been convicted, but do not expect that you will be retrying other cases. That's not the function of this trial. Now, Mr. Tieger, the extended period that you request to respond will be granted so that you ensure that a thorough job is done. There's no point in rushing this job. And the Pre-Trial Conference, when scheduled, will undoubtedly be after the 31st of August, although possibly not long after it. The important thing is that this is available for any discussions that take place in the context of the Pre-Trial Conference, that is, leading up to it or actually at that conference. Now, that completes the items I had identified. Is there anything else, Mr. Tieger, you wish to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just quickly, Your Honour. It's a matter that I raised at the previous conference, and I raise it again because it seemed to be implicated by some of the comments at today's session. It seems to me a good deal of additional information about the accused's position in relation to events at Srebrenica was adduced. That is the kind of information that I would have expected to receive in compliance with the 65 ter order. I believe last time there was reference to the -- to our review of the Defence pre-trial brief and what we considered to be a failure to comply with Rule 65. I believe at that time the Court did not have a -- had not had an opportunity to review the submission, and I would simply renew our position that the Defence pre-trial brief did not comply with Rule 65 ter (F). And there is some inconsistency clearly in any suggestion by the Defence that the Prosecution may not be focusing on fundamental issues when there's a failure to comply with a rule which is intended to advance just that objective.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Remind me what you suggested might be the remedy.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I didn't suggest a particular remedy at the time. If I recall the Court's words in general, it was that the Court would take the opportunity to review the submission, make its determination and issue an appropriate order. Presumably if it was found not to be in compliance, there would be an order to submit a pre-trial brief that, in fact, did fulfill the requirements of 65 ter (F).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The other possibility is that the Prosecution are allowed, as and when it occurs, to lead evidence that they perhaps dispensed with when some particular issue is specifically challenged without notice from the pre-trial brief. If your anxiety is that there's a lack of reassurance that it might be safe to take a bold course in relation to certain witnesses, then perhaps that's a more appropriate form of relief in this instance.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's -- well, first of all, that's one aspect of the Prosecution's concern. Another one is perhaps more -- arises more directly and more obviously out of the provisions of 65 ter (F), and that's a matter of focusing energy, resources, effort on the particular areas of concern and dispute. So there's also a resource issue in addition, but I appreciate what the Court's saying. And I also recognise that the Court may be considering exactly what a suitable remedy might be. I trust, in any event, that the Court is not surprised that I would raise this, is presumably aware of even if I don't articulate fully the ramifications of a -- a pre-trial brief that essentially circumvents the requirements and objectives of 65 ter (F) and the -- the various permutations or the various consequences that has during the course of the case. We'll obviously try to deal with it. It's not ideal. To the extent the Court can -- will consider and can craft a suitable remedy, we would urge the Court to do so, and as issues arise during the course of the case as a result of any problems arising from that deficiency, we'll bring them to the attention the Court and see what can be done accordingly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Karadzic, you heard this submission the last time, that the pre-trial brief that you submitted is inadequate in that it does not explain the basis on which you challenge material to be presented by the Prosecution. Mr. Tieger is asking the Trial Chamber to do something about it. Can I have your comments?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Lordship. Despite all the sympathy I have the opposing side, it is not my intention to do their job for them. Even the practice direction issued by the ICTY earlier this year does not make it necessary for me to do what Mr. Tieger wants me to do, and I can quote that in English: "[In English] It should be noted that since the burden is on the Prosecution to prove the case, the accused is under no obligation to agree to the narrowing of the issues in dispute and may simply refuse to agree to any facts."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is it you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm reading a quotation from the manual on developed practice. [In English] That is a manual of developed practice -- practice that has been issued earlier this year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, there's a difference in refusing to agree facts and a narrowing the issues in dispute and stating what is the basis on which you put issues in dispute. The rule that Mr. Tieger refers to requires you to state in general terms the nature of your defence. Well, you've given a very general indication of that. Then the matters with which you take issue in the Prosecutor's pre-trial brief, and then thirdly, in the case of each of these matters the reason why you take issue with it. Now, he rightly points out that you didn't undertake that exercise at all, and therefore you didn't comply with what the rules say you should do, and by doing that you admit nothing. You agree to nothing. So your reasons so far for not doing it doesn't actually persuade me.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that should I be more precise concerning details and so on, I would be doing the Prosecution's job. It is up to them to prove their allegations. I presented a very general position. I'm looking forward to this trial where we will be able to examine and scrutinise each detail, but for me now to guide them, to provide guidance for them, I have no duty to do that, and I don't think it would be rational.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that simply is a repetition of what you've already said, which doesn't really help me because it doesn't answer the criticism made. I will have to consider this with my colleagues and decide whether there is any action we ought to take at this stage. Now, I think that completes what Mr. Tieger has to raise. Is there any other matter which you wish to raise, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Lordship, at this stage when I have 1 million pages of material, 270 days of witness examination, CD and video material that I need a lot of time to go over, I cannot be more specific in response to the pre-trial brief of the Prosecution. I would use up my ammunition for nothing. So at this particular stage when I have such voluminous material, I cannot be more specific than I was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's a much better reason than you've given so far. What view my colleagues take of that I can't say at this moment. Now, is there any other matter you wish to raise?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not in relation to these issues. I have something to raise in relation to other issues if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I would like to inform that my advisor, Mr. Sladojevic, is prepared to meet today, to meet any time, but the result of that meeting will be nothing but a social one because we still do not have what Dr. Stojkovic requires. So that's something we can settle right away. I think that Mr. Sladojevic will always meet with the opposing side whenever he's expected to do that. I would like to inform you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just stop there. I mean, that's very encouraging, and I don't accept that such a meeting will achieve nothing, because it will continue to advance the case for your obtaining some of the material at least, if not all, to carry out the appropriate analysis. It may be that you will be able to devise a way of identifying a selection of the material without necessarily having it all in your hand at the moment. A satisfactory way of working out how to identify a sample, a representative sample. So that meeting would not be pointless and simply social, and I encourage you to ensure that the meeting does take place either today or tomorrow. And, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, I hope you will do your best to ensure that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Actually I see here an e-mail from Mr. Sladojevic making a proposal, but I know that we also want to speak to him on another issue, so I will have to check, and I'm actually already doing this, whether all people are in house so that we can deal with the two open issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now you've got something else, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have two or three brief matters. First of all, I'd like to inform you that our correspondence is in progress. We're expecting response from several governments. Unfortunately, some governments, not just that of Bosnia and Herzegovina, but some of the older states as well, they perceive cooperation with the Tribunal as cooperation with the OTP only. We try to avoid motions where we ask the Chamber to order such cooperation. We used a letter to High Representative in Bosnia and Herzegovina to influence the government in Bosnia and Herzegovina to start cooperating with the Defence and disclose material that they are duty-bound to disclose. There will be more material, even more sensitive material, but they refuse to cooperate even when it comes to innocent material. Now, as for Minister Bildt, Minister Bildt has still not met with my advisor --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you go into that, you know that in each instance where you have submitted a motion for a binding order in relation to any state that our practice has been to invite that state to respond to us, and the Prosecution so far have taken the position that they have no position on this. It seems to us realistic to give the states in question 14 days to respond, but we are acting on these motions as quick as we possibly can, and if there are any others they will receive the same treatment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for that. Some countries have replied, some haven't, and some replied saying that they would cooperate with the Prosecution only and that's quite unusual for us, and we will keep insisting. This was just a first wave of our requests to these governments, because this case can be clarified only if the countries that support this material and all countries that were on the ground back then provide everything that is in their possession. Now, as for Minister Bildt, my advisor travelled to Stockholm, and Mr. Bildt did not have time to meet. It was scheduled for yesterday in Brussels again and nothing happened once again. I simply need one hour of Mr. Minister Bildt's time to resolve some crucial matters concerning which he certainly has information. Minister Bildt, while he was High Representative in Bosnia and Herzegovina, required everyone to fully cooperate with The Hague Tribunal. Therefore, he should be under that obligation as well. The position of the UN is to be as accommodating as possible, and my advisor is scheduled to be in Geneva to examine some important documents there. I simply am concerned that all of these postponements will affect the beginning the trial. We need to have the material in order to come up with a proper defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm extremely concerned to hear that the meeting proposed by Mr. Bildt has not taken place, and I will instruct inquiry to be made about the reason. I will invite him to indicate what the problem is, and hopefully we can resolve this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He announced that he would see my advisor in August in Brussels, and my advisor will travel to Stockholm again if necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understood when we made an earlier order in a decision in this case that a meeting had been arranged I think for about the 14th of July, and I'm extremely disappointed that that has not taken place, and August, while it's almost upon us, is another possible five weeks away because it could be any time in August. So I will inquire what the problem is and endeavour to resolve it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that we're talking about a date in mid-August, and if you are disappointed, you can only imagine how disappointed I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you have something else?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not for the time being, Your Lordship. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I know your position on everything being conducted in public, and largely that has been respected, but there are undoubtedly benefits to be had from meetings that take place between the Prosecution and your associates. Now, they take place in private, as you -- as you know. I think there are circumstances in which I could assist the progress of this case and the production of material that you require by participating in meetings of that nature. These meetings can include you and indeed on two -- is it one? I can't remember. On one or two occasions we've had such a meeting and then published the outcome. I intend that there should be a further meeting in connection with the preparation of this case in the week beginning the 17th of August, probably the morning of the 20th of August, but I suspect that the best form of meeting then would be one in private attended also by at least one of your associates. I think that would be in your interests. So I invite you to give thought to authorising one of your associates to attend such a meeting along with yourself. You might even authorise it without your own attendance, but I'm not encouraging you to do that. You ought to play a full part in any meeting that takes place in connection with the case. So give thought to that, and we shall communicate the final date and suggested time much nearer the time. I have again found this meeting to have been productive, and I think that following upon it certain issues which were clarified today can be resolved, and I hope that all of that will prove beneficial in ensuring the fairly early start of this trial. I have nothing more to say on the likely date of the trial. The indication given the last time is that it is likely to start in September, and that remains the position. The Status Conference is now adjourned.
